summary: A clarification of how the "set data type" transaction should be used in the File Transfer Protocol. Because systems like Multics do not record file data types, a client could ask the server to convert text into Network ASCII on retrieval.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers store text in different ways, so a client can tell the other computer which form to send the file in.

subtitle: Clarifying data type conversion in file transfer protocol

tldr.problem: Systems like Multics store files without recording their data type, making it difficult to know how to interpret data during transfers.
tldr.mechanism: The FTP 'set data type' transaction lets a client specify a desired format (such as Network ASCII) and instructs the server to convert the data accordingly before sending it.
tldr.outcome: Servers can refuse conversion if they lack the capability, giving both client and server a standard way to negotiate data format.

facts.label: Solves problem for
facts.value: Systems without built-in file type metadata

today: RFC 294 updates RFC 265 and clarifies a mechanism used in early file transfer implementations. It is part of the foundational protocols that established how the network would exchange files across heterogeneous systems.

sections.title: The Problem of Data Types
sections.content:
On systems such as Multics at MIT, there is no built-in way to record what type of data a file contains. ASCII characters are stored as four 9-bit characters per 36-bit word, right-justified with the leftmost bit as zero. When transferring files to other computers, it is important to know which format the receiving system expects.

RFC 265 defined File Transfer Protocol and reserved opcode 00 for 'set data type' transactions, but its use was unclear. This RFC clarifies how the transaction should work in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: Different computers store words and letters differently, so they need to ask each other what format to use when sending files.

sections.title: Using Set Data Type
sections.content:
When a client sends a 'set data type' transaction before a retrieve request, it tells the server the format desired for the data. If the server is unable to convert the data into the requested form, it should return a 'set data type' message indicating the refusal.

For example, a Multics user can use efficient conversion programs to transform data into Network ASCII and request that conversion when retrieving files from a Multics server. The server can either perform the conversion or inform the client it cannot.
sections.plainLanguage: Before asking for a file, the client says 'send it in this format please,' and the server either does it or says it cannot.

sections.title: Common Scenarios
sections.content:
A client might set data type to Network ASCII (type 02) before storing files, expecting the server to keep them in that format. On retrieval, the client again sets the data type to Network ASCII and receives the file in that format.

Alternatively, if a server cannot provide the requested format, it replies with 'set data type' 00 (bit-stream), meaning it will send the file as stored without conversion. The client can then either accept the raw data or request a different format.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask for Network ASCII and the server can do that, you get it. If it cannot, it sends the raw file instead.

references.text: Bhushan, A., et al., "File Transfer Protocol", RFC 265, November 1971.
